g.text: What and Where — the transformation, and the slice it runs over
one sum, four windowings: global 45 · fixed 4 windows · sliding totals 78 · sessions a=3 b=2
seed: tools/stream_seed.js · window [12:00, 12:02) = 19
WHAT — THE COMPUTATION, WITH THE WINDOW HELD FIXED
four different WHATs, all over the same WHERE
sum of v over window [12:00, 12:02)
count over the same window
4 events
max of v over the same window
count DISTINCT key over the same window
2 (keys a, b)
Every row reads the same 4 events. Only the computation changed, and the window was never mentioned.
In the Beam model this is a transform in a directed graph: it says what comes out, and nothing about boundaries.
Step 1/4 — WHAT is one choice: the transformation
Hold the window still and vary the computation: four answers from the same 4 events. That is "what" — a sum, a count, a max, a distinct count.
Notice the last row needs the KEY field while the first needs only `v`; the transform decides which fields matter, and still says nothing about
where a boundary falls.
What and Where — the transformation, and the slice it runs over
one sum, four windowings: global 45 · fixed 4 windows · sliding totals 78 · sessions a=3 b=2
seed: tools/stream_seed.js · window [12:00, 12:02) = 19
WHERE — THE SAME SUM, OVER FOUR DIFFERENT WINDOWINGS
one transform (sum of v); four answers to "over what slice?"
global window (all of event time)
1 result: 45
fixed 120s windows
4 results: 19, 11, 7, 8 (total 45)
sliding 120s wide, every 60s
7 results, totalling 78
session windows, 120s gap
key a: 3 sessions · key b: 2 sessions
Read the third row twice: the sliding results total 78, not 45. No data was duplicated — the WINDOWS overlap, so most events are counted in two
of them.
The fixed and global rows both total 45 because their windows partition event time. Overlap is a property of the windowing, not of the data.
Step 2/4 — WHERE is a separate choice: the windowing
Same transform throughout — `sum(v)` — and four different shapes of answer. The sliding row is the one that surprises people: its results add up
to 78 against a dataset containing 45, because each event falls in up to 2 overlapping windows. Partitioning windows preserve the total;
overlapping ones do not, by design.
What and Where — the transformation, and the slice it runs over
one sum, four windowings: global 45 · fixed 4 windows · sliding totals 78 · sessions a=3 b=2
seed: tools/stream_seed.js · window [12:00, 12:02) = 19
WHAT x WHERE — EVERY COMBINATION IS LEGAL
the grid is filled in for key a; no cell is forbidden and no cell is implied by another
global
fixed 120s
sessions 120s
sum(v)
count
distinct key
Nine cells, nine legal pipelines. Changing the row does not constrain the column and the reverse is also true.
This is why the book asks the two questions separately: a design that answers only one of them is not half-specified, it is unspecified.
Step 3/4 — the two axes really are independent
Nine cells and every one is a real pipeline you could run. The grid is the argument for separating the questions: "we sum purchases" names a row
and leaves the answer undetermined, and "we use session windows" names a column and does the same. Both are needed before any number exists.
What and Where — the transformation, and the slice it runs over
one sum, four windowings: global 45 · fixed 4 windows · sliding totals 78 · sessions a=3 b=2
seed: tools/stream_seed.js · window [12:00, 12:02) = 19
A MAPREDUCE JOB, IN THESE TERMS
the same four questions, answered by a batch job without being asked
WHAT
the map and reduce functions — explicit, and the part everyone discusses
WHERE
the input file — ONE implicit window covering all 45 of the data
WHEN
end of input — implicit, and the reason it never comes up
HOW
nothing to relate: one window emits once, so there are no panes
Batch answers all four. It just answers three of them by accident, because the input ended.
So the streaming model is not four new questions — it is the same four, with the defaults removed.
Step 4/4 — batch already answers both — implicitly
This is why the four questions are not streaming jargon. A MapReduce job over one file answers WHERE with "the file" and WHEN with "when I finish
reading it", and both are correct — they are just invisible. Take away the end of the input and all three defaults stop existing at once, which is
the whole difficulty.
